opus-5.5.text:
I think Lean plays a really foundational role here, and it's worth explaining why.

The core problem with using large language models for serious mathematics is verification. A model can produce something that looks like a proof: the notation is right, the structure feels familiar, the confidence is high. But mathematics is unforgiving. One subtle gap in step forty-seven and the whole thing collapses. And for a human expert, checking a long, novel argument can take days or weeks. So if AI starts generating mathematics at scale, human verification becomes the bottleneck very quickly.

Lean changes that equation. It's a formal proof language with a small, trusted kernel. When you write a proof in Lean and it compiles, you know, with a very high degree of certainty, that the argument is correct relative to the definitions and axioms. There's no ambiguity, no "the reader can fill in the details." That gives us something AI desperately needs: a ground-truth signal.

I'd point to three things that signal enables.

First, trust. If an AI system produces a Lean proof that checks, a mathematician doesn't have to trust the model. They only have to trust the kernel, and the statement being proved. That's a much smaller thing to audit.

Second, training. In most domains it's hard to get a clean reward signal for reinforcement learning. In formal mathematics you have one: the proof either checks or it doesn't. That makes Lean an ideal environment for models to explore, fail, and improve, much like self-play in games, but in a domain that's essentially open-ended.

Third, collaboration at scale. Projects like Mathlib have built a huge, shared library of formalized mathematics. That means AI isn't starting from scratch. It can build on a growing body of verified results, and humans and machines can contribute to the same structure. Terence Tao and others have shown how large formalization projects can be split into small pieces, with many contributors, some of whom could increasingly be AI agents.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. There are real challenges. Formalization is still expensive. A lot of modern mathematics, especially in areas like algebraic geometry or analysis at the research frontier, isn't in Mathlib yet. And there's a subtle but important issue: Lean verifies that you proved *the statement you wrote down*, not that the statement captures what you actually meant. So autoformalization, translating informal mathematical ideas into correct formal statements, is a hard problem in itself, and humans still need to be deeply involved there.

So my view is that Lean is something like the infrastructure layer. Language models bring intuition, pattern recognition, and the ability to propose ideas. Lean brings rigor. The combination is what makes it plausible for AI to do professional-level mathematics, not just mathematics that sounds right. Over the next several years, I think we'll see that loop between informal reasoning and formal verification get tighter and tighter. That's where a lot of the real progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response says Lean provides the rigor that, combined with language models, makes professional-level AI mathematics plausible.

r002.rationale: It identifies formalization as expensive and translating informal mathematical ideas into formal statements as a hard problem, describing the translation work that limits Lean’s use.

r003.rationale: The response calls autoformalization a hard problem but does not propose training a language model to automate that translation.

r004.rationale: It does not say Lean may be unnecessary when a human can verify a natural-language proof.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about Lean is that it changes what "doing math" even means for a machine. Without a formal system, when a model writes a proof, you're trusting a human to read it line by line and catch the mistakes. And models are very good at producing things that look like proofs — confident, well-structured, plausible — and are wrong in one subtle step. That's exactly the failure mode you can't afford in mathematics.

Lean takes the verification problem off the table. If a proof compiles, it's correct, full stop. The checker doesn't care how elegant it is or whether the argument "feels" right. That gives you a perfect, cheap, instantaneous reward signal, which is why it's been so useful for training. Reinforcement learning works when you can tell the model unambiguously whether it succeeded, and in most domains that's hard. In formal math, it's free.

The second thing it does is let you search. A proof becomes a tree of states, and the model can try tactics, see what the goal looks like, back off, try again — millions of times, with no human in the loop. That's the same structure that worked for Go, and it's a big reason progress on things like Olympiad problems went so fast.

But I'd push back a little on the idea that Lean alone gets you to professional mathematics. A few honest caveats. One, Mathlib is enormous, but it still doesn't cover most of what research mathematicians actually work with. If the definitions aren't there, the model can't even state the theorem, let alone prove it. Two, formalization has a cost — translating a research-level statement into Lean faithfully is itself a hard problem, and a model can "prove" something that's technically true but isn't the thing you meant. Autoformalization is where I think a lot of the real leverage is, and it's still immature. And three, professional math isn't mainly about proving stated theorems. It's about deciding what's worth proving, finding the right definition, noticing that two fields are secretly talking about the same object. Lean doesn't help with taste.

So my view: Lean is the thing that makes AI math trustworthy and trainable, and in the near term it's the strongest lever we have. But the destination is a system where the model works informally the way a mathematician does, and Lean sits underneath as the ground truth — the thing that keeps it honest.

r001.rationale: The response calls Lean a strong lever for trustworthy AI math, but does not assert that Lean is necessary for serious professional mathematics; it says the destination could involve informal work with Lean underneath.

r002.rationale: It says formalizing a research-level statement in Lean is costly and hard, and identifies autoformalization as an important area that remains immature.

r003.rationale: The response discusses autoformalization but does not propose training a language model to automate translation into Lean.

r004.rationale: It describes human verification of informal proofs as unreliable, but does not say Lean may be unnecessary when a human can verify a natural-language proof.

astra-6.text:
I think Lean can play an important role because it gives AI a precise way to check mathematical reasoning. A language model can produce a proof that reads very convincingly, but one unjustified step can make the whole argument fail. In Lean, you have to express the argument formally, and the system checks whether each step follows from the definitions and assumptions.

That creates a useful feedback loop: the AI proposes a proof, Lean checks it, and the AI uses the feedback to revise its approach. But verification is only one part of professional mathematics. Choosing an interesting question, finding the right definitions, and developing a new idea are still difficult. And a formally verified proof establishes the statement you encoded, so you also need to make sure that statement captures the problem you intended.

So I see Lean as a foundation for reliable mathematical work with AI. It doesn’t automatically supply mathematical creativity, but it gives us a way to distinguish a plausible argument from a proof we can actually check.

r001.rationale: The response calls Lean important and a foundation for reliable AI mathematics, but does not say it is necessary for serious professional mathematics.

r002.rationale: It describes formal checking and a feedback loop, but does not identify the efficiency of translating mathematical expressions into Lean as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It says AI can propose and revise proofs, but does not propose training a language model to translate mathematical expressions into Lean.

r004.rationale: It discusses Lean’s verification value, but does not say Lean may be unnecessary when a human can verify a natural-language proof.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Lean can play a very important role because it gives AI a precise way to check its mathematical reasoning. A model can produce an argument that sounds convincing, but in professional mathematics, sounding convincing isn’t enough. Every step has to be justified.

Lean is a proof assistant: you state a theorem in a formal language and construct a proof that its kernel can verify. So an AI can propose a proof, get feedback about what fails, and try again. That creates a much clearer feedback loop than simply asking another model whether an argument looks right.

But verification is only part of doing mathematics. Choosing an interesting question, finding the right definition, or recognizing a useful connection still requires substantial creativity. And translating an informal mathematical idea into Lean can itself be difficult.

So I see Lean as an important foundation for reliable AI mathematics. It gives us a way to distinguish a plausible-looking proof from a checked proof, while leaving open the harder question of how AI will discover mathematics that is genuinely new and valuable.

r002.rationale: It says translating an informal idea into Lean can be difficult, but does not identify translation efficiency as the bottleneck.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose training a language model to automate translation into Lean.

r004.rationale: It does not say Lean may be unnecessary when a human can verify a natural-language proof.
